lines.watchItem: Leading-edge wafer demand keeps running ahead of what the chain can deliver: the four largest US cloud buyers are guiding to roughly $725 billion of 2026 capital spending, Google Cloud's contracted backlog jumped past $500 billion, and NVIDIA guided its next quarter to $91 billion. Watch whether those order books convert on schedule or slip, because wafer-start plans across leading nodes ride on them.

Advanced packaging is still the gate on how much accelerator revenue can actually ship, with capacity booked out and lead times of 52 to 78 weeks even as monthly output climbs toward 125,000 to 130,000 wafers. The exposure now runs the other way too: forecasters expect the supply-demand gap to narrow from about 20% to about 10% by end-2026, so watch how fast tightness converts into normal allocation.

Stacked memory looks like the tighter of the two limits: it is sold out through 2026 with much of 2027 pre-booked, one supplier holds 56.4% of that market, and Micron says it can meet only half to two-thirds of customer demand. If memory, not packaging, sets accelerator volumes, packaging slots can free up faster than the order book implies.

The leading-node customer base is shifting away from a single dominant name: NVIDIA's accelerator share is projected to fall from 87% in 2024 toward 75% in 2026, custom cloud silicon is growing 44.6% against 16.1% for merchant parts, and AMD has booked gigawatt-scale commitments with Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. Watch whether the mix broadens into more customers or simply moves volume to the two design houses that run about 95% of custom AI chip work.

Packaging output leans on very few names: the top three clients take over 85%, with one at roughly 60% and another at about 11% that it splits between its server processors and its accelerators. Any one of them trimming orders leaves capacity that is slow to refill, and one is reported to be weighing a move of some next-generation output to a rival packaging method.

Pricing power across the chain is holding: TSMC posted a 67.7% gross margin and lifted full-year growth guidance above 40%, NVIDIA held a 75% non-GAAP gross margin, and median GB200 rental rates are up about 42% year over year. Watch whether end-market rental prices stay firm as the second-half accelerator wave lands, since that is what carries pricing power back upstream.

Second-source activity is picking up on several fronts at once: Intel's foundry revenue rose 31% to $5.8 billion with a first external customer named, Intel's inference GPU skips high-bandwidth memory to sidestep the packaging queue, and Anthropic is in early talks with Samsung about a 2-nanometer custom chip. Each one is a small piece of demand that could route around the current leading-node path.

The demand behind those wafer plans carries policy and financing strings: China data-center revenue fell to $4.55 billion from $9.66 billion, roughly 210,000 GPUs now sit under vendor-backed purchase programs, and Alphabet funded its build-out with $49.6 billion of equity and $20.3 billion of notes into its first negative free cash flow. Investors marked down AI-infrastructure names on the bigger capex numbers, which is the early tell to watch on order durability.
